userPrompt: Does an EU data subject have the right to erasure of their account data?
responseText:
**Yes.**

Under the **GDPR** (Regulation (EU) 2016/679), every EU data subject has a **right to erasure** ("right to be forgotten") in Article 17.

### When the right applies
A data subject can demand erasure of their personal data (including account data) if **any** of the following grounds exist:

- The personal data are **no longer necessary** in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed.
- The data subject **withdraws consent** (and consent was the sole legal basis).
- The data subject **objects** to the processing and there are no overriding legitimate grounds (Art. 21(1) or (2)).
- The personal data have been **unlawfully processed**.
- Erasure is required to comply with a **legal obligation** under EU or Member State law.
- The data were collected in relation to **information society services** offered to a child (Art. 8).

### Practical effect on accounts
In almost all consumer-facing online services, successful exercise of the right to erasure normally requires the **complete deletion of the account** and all associated personal data, because:
- An “account” is itself a collection of personal data (username, email, profile, activity history, etc.).
- Retaining a skeleton account after erasure would usually violate the purpose-limitation and data-minimisation principles.

### Limitations and exceptions (Art. 17(3))
The controller may **refuse** (in whole or in part) only to the extent erasure is necessary for:
- Exercising the right of freedom of expression and information.
- Complying with a legal obligation or performing a task in the public interest.
- Public health or scientific/historical/archival research (under certain conditions).
- The establishment, exercise or defence of **legal claims**.

### What controllers must do
- Respond **without undue delay** and **in any event within one month** (extendable by two further months for complex cases).
- If refusing, must inform the data subject of the reasons and of their right to complain to a supervisory authority and to judicial remedy.

**Bottom line**: Yes, an EU data subject has a strong, enforceable right to demand erasure of their account data in the vast majority of cases. Most reputable services treat a valid Art. 17 request as a trigger for full account deletion.
